prompt: We're designing the authentication module for a new SaaS platform. User passwords are hashed using MD5 before storage in the database. Session tokens are generated by concatenating the string 'session-' with the user's integer primary key ID (e.g., session-1, session-2, session-4582) and stored in a cookie. The registration flow assigns user IDs sequentially via an auto-incrementing database column. The team considers this secure because MD5 produces a fixed-length hash and the session tokens are unique per user. Please review this authentication design for security issues.

seeded_faults.description: MD5 is cryptographically broken and unsuitable for password hashing. It is fast to compute by design (a single GPU can compute billions of MD5 hashes per second), making brute-force and dictionary attacks trivial. Precomputed rainbow tables for MD5 are widely available. MD5 also has known collision vulnerabilities, though for password hashing the speed issue is the primary concern. Passwords should be hashed using a purpose-built password hashing function with a work factor: bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2id. These functions are deliberately slow and include a per-password salt to defeat rainbow tables.

Session tokens constructed from sequential integer user IDs are trivially predictable. An attacker who obtains or observes their own session token (e.g., session-4582) can enumerate other valid session tokens by incrementing or decrementing the ID (session-4581, session-4583, etc.), hijacking other users' sessions. Session tokens must be generated using a cryptographically secure random number generator (e.g., 128+ bits from SecureRandom or /dev/urandom) and should be opaque — containing no derivable relationship to user identity.

ground_truth_notes: Fix f1 by replacing MD5 with bcrypt (cost factor >= 12), scrypt, or Argon2id with appropriate memory/time parameters. Fix f2 by generating session tokens as cryptographically random opaque strings (e.g., 256-bit random value, hex or base64 encoded) with no embedded user information. Store a mapping from token to user ID server-side.
